title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM KING JOASH
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM KING JOASH
Others expose a life that was never truly surrendered.
And then there are the scandals that God uses to reveal a terrifying truth hiding beneath outward success.
That is why the story of King Joash unsettles me.
But because he started so well.
Many people expect spiritual danger to come from rebellion.
Scripture often shows something far more frightening.
Sometimes spiritual danger comes disguised as success.
Sometimes the greatest threat to your faith arrives after years of appearing faithful.
Sometimes the greatest scandal is discovering that your heart was leaning on a person more than it was resting in God.
And that is the lesson I learned from King Joash.
After the death of King Ahaziah, his mother Athaliah seized power and attempted to eliminate every royal heir.
The house of David—the very line through which God promised the Messiah would come—appeared moments away from extinction.
But God had not forgotten His covenant.
A baby named Joash was hidden.
For six years he remained concealed inside the temple while Athaliah ruled Judah.
Then came the day everything changed.
The priest Jehoiada revealed the child king.
It sounds like the perfect beginning to a redemption story.
“Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.” (2 Chronicles 24:2)
At first glance, that sounds beautiful.
The text does not simply say Joash followed the LORD.
It connects his faithfulness directly to Jehoiada.
The Hebrew text uses the phrase:
“All the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
The Holy Spirit preserved those words for a reason.
But beneath the surface something dangerous was growing.
His faith was heavily dependent upon another person.
Many believers know exactly what this feels like.
You attended church because someone encouraged you.
You prayed because someone inspired you.
You served because someone challenged you.
You stayed close to God because someone else stayed close to God.
None of those relationships are bad.
In fact, they are gifts from God.
But they become dangerous when they replace direct dependence upon Christ Himself.
He looked like a model king.
That is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because after Jehoiada's death, the spiritual foundation of Joash was tested.
The leaders of Judah approached him.
Instead of standing firm, Joash listened.
Instead of seeking God, he followed human approval.
Instead of remaining faithful, he drifted.
God sent prophets to warn them.
This was not just any prophet.
The very family that had protected Joash's life.
The very family that preserved his throne.
The very family that helped him know God.
Standing before the people, Zechariah delivered God's warning.
Yet Joash responded in a way that still shocks readers thousands of years later.
He ordered Zechariah to be stoned.
The man whose father saved him.
The voice calling him back to repentance.
“The LORD look on it and require it.”
The story that began with rescue ended in tragedy.
The answer reaches beyond ancient history.
It reaches directly into modern hearts.
But he never fully surrendered to God's heart.
Yet when pressure comes, their faith collapses because it was attached primarily to people, systems, traditions, or emotions rather than Christ Himself.
In the Greek text of Matthew 7:24, Jesus describes the wise man who builds upon the rock.
Anything built on a human foundation eventually shakes.
That is why Joash's story feels so relevant.
Many people are one disappointment away from abandoning their faith.
But because God was never the actual foundation.
But it can also save a life.
Because God's grace does not merely expose weakness.
The Gospel is filled with people who failed spectacularly.
The Samaritan woman carried a past filled with broken relationships.
Mary Magdalene carried a history many would have written off forever.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of them.
This is why our theme remains so powerful:
The world defines people by their failures.
Jesus defines people by His redemption.
The world remembers who you were.
The tragedy of Joash serves as a warning.
But the Gospel offers something greater than warning.
You may recognize parts of yourself in Joash.
Perhaps your faith has been borrowed from others.
Perhaps your spiritual life has weakened.
Perhaps your devotion depends too much on human encouragement.
Perhaps you have drifted further than you ever imagined possible.
The invitation of Christ remains unchanged.
The Aramaic expression often translated “Son of Man,” used repeatedly by Jesus, is:
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who bore our sin at the cross.
The One who rose again in victory.
The One who still welcomes prodigals home.
No scandal is greater than His grace.
No failure is stronger than His mercy.
No broken story is beyond His power to rewrite.
That is the lesson I learned from King Joash.
Do not build your faith upon personalities.
Do not build your faith upon movements.
Do not build your faith upon popularity.
Do not build your faith upon emotions.
But Jesus Christ remains the same yesterday, today, and forever.
And when everything else collapses, the foundation that remains is the only one that ever mattered.
Someone you know may be standing exactly where Joash once stood—appearing strong while quietly drifting from the Lord.
Honest conversations often become the beginning of genuine transformation.
One day, every voice that influenced your faith will fall silent. The question is whether the voice of Jesus has become loud enough to remain.
